How Voyager Tracker works

Every live number on this site comes from one small calculation that runs in your browser. This page shows exactly what it does, what data it starts from, how well it matches JPL’s own predictions, and where it stops being reliable.

The short version

This tracker uses a calculated estimate rather than direct NASA telemetry. It is not NASA’s official telemetry, not a JPL tracking system and not an interface to the Deep Space Network. It starts from official JPL Horizons data and does the rest itself — transparently.

Reference data

  • State vectors (position and velocity) of Voyager 1 and 2 for 2026-09-01, from JPL Horizons targets −31 and −32.
  • A monthly table of the Sun’s offset from the solar system’s centre of mass, 2020–2040 (JPL Horizons).
  • Monthly distance and speed of both probes from launch to 2035 (JPL Horizons), used by the charts, the timeline and the date calculator.
  • Instrument status and mission events copied from NASA publications (last checked 2026-08-04).

Nothing is fetched from NASA while you browse: the reference data is bundled with the site and regenerated by a script in the project’s public repository. GitHub

The calculation, step by step

  1. 1. Read the clock

    Your device’s clock gives the current time in UTC. The model works in seconds elapsed since the reference epoch; the 69.184-second difference between UTC and the TDB timescale used by JPL is applied.

    Δt = (now_UTC − epoch_TDB + 69.184 s)

  2. 2. Move each spacecraft forward

    Starting from the position r₀ and velocity v₀ that JPL Horizons gives for 2026-09-01 (measured from the solar system’s centre of mass), the position is advanced with a third-order Taylor series that includes the gentle pull of the Sun and planets (acceleration a₀ and its rate of change j₀).

    r(t) = r₀ + v₀·Δt + ½·a₀·Δt² + ⅙·j₀·Δt³, a₀ = −μ·r₀ / |r₀|³

  3. 3. Find the Sun and Earth

    The Sun itself wobbles around the solar system’s centre of mass by up to about 1.4 million kilometres (2020–2040), mostly because of Jupiter; its offset is interpolated from a monthly JPL table. Earth’s position around the Sun comes from the standard low-precision solar formula published in the Astronomical Almanac, rotated to the same J2000 reference frame.

  4. 4. Measure the distances

    Distance from the Sun and distance from Earth are straight-line distances between the positions above. Because Earth’s position changes through the year, the Earth distance rises and falls by up to about 0.8 AU relative to the Sun distance.

    d_Earth = |r_spacecraft − r_Earth|, d_Sun = |r_spacecraft − r_Sun|

  5. 5. Speed and light time

    Speed relative to the Sun is the length of the propagated velocity vector. The rate at which the Earth distance changes also includes Earth’s own orbital velocity, which is why it can be negative. One-way light time is the Earth distance divided by the speed of light.

    t_light = d_Earth / 299,792.458 km/s

  6. 6. Convert units

    1 AU = 149,597,870.7 km (IAU 2012 definition); 1 mile = 1.609344 km; light-hours and light-days use the exact speed of light. Rounding happens only when numbers are displayed.

How often the numbers update

The tracker re-runs the calculation about ten times per second, so the counters move smoothly; this is a fresh calculation for the new instant, not a download. The map redraws once a minute and milestone countdowns tick once a second. The reference data changes only when it is regenerated from JPL and the site is rebuilt; the date of the last build is shown in the footer of every page.

How accurate is it? Validation against JPL

The model was compared with JPL Horizons’ own geocentric distances every five days from 2024 to 2031 (validated 2026-09-25). The table shows the largest difference found in each year.

Maximum model error by year, km
YearVoyager 1 max errorVoyager 2 max error
202414,333 km11,597 km
202525,703 km23,066 km
202624,096 km22,253 km
202717,982 km15,809 km
202817,215 km16,351 km
202911,878 km9,772 km
203013,320 km15,985 km
203120,531 km36,176 km

The worst case, 36,176 km, is about 0.00024 AU — roughly 0.12 light-seconds, or under 0.0002% of Voyager 2’s distance. As an independent check, the model puts Voyager 1’s crossing of one light-day from Earth on 2026-11-18; NASA gives 18 November 2026.

Why not zero? The remaining difference comes mostly from the simplified formula for Earth’s position, which is accurate to about 0.01°. An earlier version of this site, which advanced a fixed distance at a fixed speed and ignored Earth’s orbit, was off by roughly 6 AU; that is documented on the Updates page. Updates

Accuracy of the historical reconstruction

The Date Explorer and the two-date comparison rebuild the distance from Earth for any date from monthly JPL positions. Compared with JPL’s own distances every 10 days:

PeriodVoyager 1 median / maxVoyager 2 median / max
1977–1989 (planetary flybys)15,306 / 3,112,143 km21,659 / 4,254,203 km
1990–19997,801 / 29,524 km8,513 / 32,486 km
2000–20096,436 / 23,174 km7,018 / 23,266 km
2010–20195,136 / 22,195 km5,086 / 21,435 km
2020–20346,840 / 25,513 km6,184 / 24,305 km

The large maximum in 1977–1989 happens around the planetary flybys, when the spacecraft’s path bends sharply within days and a straight line between two monthly samples cannot follow it. Outside those weeks the reconstruction stays within a few tens of thousands of kilometres.

Methodology changelog

  1. v1 · 2026-09-05

    Fixed 2026 starting distances advanced at a constant speed; distance from Earth assumed equal to distance from the Sun. Later found to be about 5–6 AU off.

  2. v2 · 2026-09-25

    JPL Horizons barycentric state vectors propagated with a third-order Taylor series; Sun offset from the barycentre and Earth’s orbit modelled; validated against JPL for 2024–2031.

  3. v2.1 · 2026-09-25

    Monthly JPL position vectors added so the distance from Earth and the signal delay can be reconstructed for any date from 1977 to 2034 (Date Explorer, Compare two dates); this reconstruction is validated separately against JPL, with results published below.

Limitations

  • If your device clock is wrong, the numbers are wrong by the same amount of time (Voyager 1 moves about 61,000 km per hour).
  • The model is validated only for 2024–2031. Far from the reference epoch the Taylor series slowly drifts; the reference data will be refreshed from JPL well before that matters.
  • JPL’s positions after today are themselves predictions. Real spacecraft occasionally fire thrusters for attitude control; those tiny effects are not modelled.
  • Distances are geometric (where the spacecraft is now), not corrected for the time light takes to travel. Some official tools report light-time-corrected values, which can differ slightly.
  • Instrument status and mission events are not calculated: they are copied by hand from NASA publications and dated (currently 2026-08-04). They can lag behind NASA’s latest news.

Why other sites may show different numbers

  • Distance from Earth vs. distance from the Sun — they differ by up to about 1 AU.
  • An older starting value advanced at a fixed speed, which can drift by millions of kilometres.
  • Ignoring Earth’s orbit, so the Earth distance never shows its yearly swing.
  • Light-time correction, time scales and rounding.

What each label means

OfficialPublished by NASA/JPL and cited: mission dates, encounters, instrument status, JPL Horizons reference vectors.
Calculated / estimatedProduced by this site’s model from official reference data: current distances, speeds, light times, milestones, separation between the probes.
Historical dataJPL Horizons monthly samples used in charts and the date calculator; future months are JPL predictions.
EducationalExplanatory diagrams such as the Earth-orbit schematic and the scale ruler. They illustrate an idea and are not drawn to scale unless stated.
Hypothetical“What if” comparisons such as travel time at airliner speed. Illustrations of scale, not predictions.
